utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, Alexis Demirdjian, Joanna Korner, and our Case Manager, Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I raise a short matter, please, which will require to us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only matter can I just raise with Your Honours. Yesterday when we were discussing adjudicated facts, I pointed out that, at the moment, we were undertaking the major exercise of working out what evidence would be needed to cover the adjudicated facts which were either not granted or rescinded. But as Your Honours know, we have put in an application for leave to appeal the decision and indeed still outstanding is the Defence's application for leave to appeal on his intercept decision. I know there are still a large number of decisions outstanding but, Your Honours, given that the trial is moving forward relatively fast I wonder whether Your Honours could give any indication of when we could expect the decision on our application for leave to appeal because it makes a difference obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, all can I say at this point is that we are not -- we haven't forgotten that there are these outstanding motions and they're in the process of being worked on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, all I can say is perhaps can I ask if Your Honours have an order of priority, obviously ones that affect witnesses are upcoming such as timing are most urgent, but perhaps Your Honours might consider moving that up the priority list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've noted your concern, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I promised a condensed submission today for -- on the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of the Stanisic Defence is that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is very clear on the matter. Basically in this particular case the pre-trial decision on adjudicated facts was -- states that the adjudicated facts are rebuttal at the trial. So that is the -- that is the situation. There's -- nothing has changed in that respect, and the jurisprudence is on that -- on that particular subject, very clear. Now, in our Defence pre-trial brief and throughout these proceedings, we said, we gave notice to the Prosecutor that unless it is agreed, we challenge all OTP evidence. That is in our pre-trial brief, and we repeated this over and over in the course of these proceedings. The -- the problem, as I see, is that -- that -- that somehow the adjudicated facts are -- are confused with the stipulation, and it's not the stipulation. It is a well-founded presumption for the accuracy of the fact which may be challenged and rebutted by the accused. That is the adjudicated facts. Now, this is exactly what the Lukic and Lukic decision says, under paragraph 15 that Ms. Korner was citing -- or mentioning yesterday. The -- the -- the Trial Chamber said exactly this in paragraph 15: "A chamber establishes a well-founded presumption for the accuracy of this fact. However, it is well established that an adjudicated fact may be challenged at the trial. And furthermore, the judicial notice of adjudicated fact does not shift the ultimate burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt which remains with the Prosecution." I think it cannot be more clearer than this. My reading of -- of the decision in Lukic and Lukic is that this is a very specific situation. It doesn't change the jurisprudence of this Tribunal at all. Namely, this -- this particular case was a direct perpetration case, and that is what the Trial Chamber specifically emphasises in paragraph 19. And what they are saying is that, in fact, the Prosecution in that case was for months in advance put on the notice that this -- this evidence concerning the -- the fire will be challenged by the Defence. And, in fact, that the -- that the -- in the opinion of the Trial Chamber the Prosecution already brought sufficient evidence to back up their position on that particular fire. And that is the reason why they -- why they denied the Prosecution request for rebuttal evidence. So, in that respect, as I say, we have -- we have challenged this. The jurisprudence is that the -- the -- the Defence is not required to specify their -- their challenges to the adjudicated facts. It is sufficient that the Defence state, as we did, we challenge all adjudicated facts, and we will rebut them in the course of this trial with the evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I ask this, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- as I understand the jurisprudence, aware of the necessity to continually remind one's self and is especially so for the side relying on adjudicated facts and secondarily the Trial Chamber to remind one's self of not falling into the trap of conflating adjudicated facts with facts which may be stipulated or agreed but on a practical level the -- as the trial progresses inasmuch as a trial is, as I have said on a number of occasions, a dynamic process, that something may have become agreed although initially entering the court, as it were, dressed in the guise of adjudicated facts, is there a process by which the side opposite can then confirm to -- to the side opposite and to the Chamber that in fact these -- these matters have moved into the category of agreed facts or stipulated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I am aware of the jurisprudence, that is between the parties. Of course, at any time the Prosecution can approach the Defence and ask for particular adjudicated fact, and based on the developments in the trial, they can -- they can offer us, that we stipulate that fact. That is, of course. And then if we do stipulate, then it becomes stipulated fact. That goes without saying, in my opinion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... on the law. I'm not sure Mr. Zecevic is reading from which decision because the decision I have in the Lukic case is the 25th of March, 2009 which was a decision on the application by the Prosecution to call rebuttal evidence. Your Honours, the first case on this on which the other decisions are followed is, in fact, a case from Rwanda, Karemera and others, 16th of June, 2006, and at paragraph 42, the -- this was said: "The Appeals Chamber reiterates that judicial notice does not shift the ultimate burden of persuasion, which remains with the Prosecution." Which, of course, is obvious. "In the case of judicial notice ..." -- and, really, adjudicated facts are effectively that, the ultimate burden of persuasion which -- "judicial notice does not shift the ultimate burden of persuasion, which remains with the Prosecution. In the case of judicial notice ... the effect is only to relieve the Prosecution of its initial burden to produce evidence on the point ..." And it's the following sentence which is important: "The Defence may then put the point into question by introducing reliable" -- and I emphasise the word -- "reliable and credible evidence to the contrary." And that is what was followed in the Lukic case. As I say, the one I've got is the decision on rebuttal evidence, 25th of March, 2009. So it's not sufficient simply to say, as Mr. Pantelic said yesterday, We dispute everything; or as Mr. Zecevic said, In our final -- In our pre-trial brief, we said we disputed everything. It's not only not a proper way of dealing with matters, it is actually not true because it's -- it's become apparent that there are many matters which are not in dispute. And the third thing is, I absolutely agree that adjudicated facts are not the same as agreed facts between the parties. Your Honours or certainly Judge Harhoff may recall that way back before the trial started we gave to the Defence a set of facts of stipulations as the Americans call it, agreed facts as I would call it, and asked them to agree. I mean, we were told that they were unable to agree any, and I think that was conveyed to Judge Hall, so we have been unable to reach agreement save in respect maybe of the legal library if it ever comes into evidence. But the concern that I have is this. That if there are adjudicated facts, we would invite Your Honours to say that the Defence have to call reliable and credible evidence rather than simply saying we dispute it or leave reliable and credible evidence through our witnesses. They don't necessarily have to call it themselves to show that those adjudicated facts cannot be relied on. So that is the situation. Of course, as I say, the ultimate burden of proofing the case still rests with us. But at the moment we are in a -- in a -- in a difficult position in that as I said to Your Honours yesterday, and that's what caused this application by me, is that we're only learning what particular fact is in dispute as and when witnesses come from a particular area or to deal with a particular aspect of the case which at present is covered by adjudicated facts, and that you may think is neither efficient nor indeed a very fair method of proceeding because it means the whole time we're having to re-adjust and start looking for evidence which we didn't appreciate that we would have to call, and as I say, a blanket we challenge everything that the Prosecution wants to is, as I say, not only unhelpful and not a proper way of proceeding but positively in this case actually not right. So that's the situation. And, Your Honours, I did make some inquiries overnight over the question Judge Hall asked me whether there had been another case in this Tribunal where an order that the Defence should say specifically which adjudicated facts they actually challenge. There hasn't been basically because there haven't been that many cases since adjudicated facts were used. And so, as far as I know, there's been no such order. But that's -- that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may of assistance giving the reference to the decision which I was citing from. Your Honours, I was citing from the final decision in Lukic and Lukic on the subject, and that is the decision on motion for reconsideration or certification to appeal the decision on rebuttal witness, dated 9 of April 2009. Case Prosecutor Milan Lukic versus [sic] Sredoje Lukic. That is the decision I was citing for as I felt that the final decision on the matter would be the most appropriate one. Now just two short comments on what Ms. Korner was commenting just. It is -- it is my recollection that the Rwanda decision was about the Defence case, so it's a bit -- it's a bit different aspect that was -- that the Trial Chamber had in view in -- in that respect, the one which -- which Ms. Korner was citing. And the -- and the second thing is, Your Honour, you will remember that there is an number of facts that we agreed upon. It is not true that we are challenging everything. We agreed upon the facts which we feel are agreeable. We are not going to agree to the facts which we think are not -- are rebuttable or that we are going to challenge and which are important for our case. And I don't -- I mean, apart from that, I don't have anything to add. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, for the record, as I said yesterday, and I really do not see a -- grounds for submission this morning submission of Ms. Korner. Zupljanin Defence denies all adjudicated facts. We have a right to do that. And in addition to that during the Prosecution case, we showed in our cross-examination that a number of facts are actually challenged. For example, Ms. Korner recently informed us off the record that she is not going to lead evidence regarding the split of BH MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Your Honours, I object to and I will not have, as Mr. Pantelic says, off-the-record conversations if they're going to be repeated in court. If Mr. Pantelic wants to stop having communication out of court then he can continue. But I do not consider that chat -- what I call robing room chat, is something that should be repeated in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can have your time later for reply. So the proper way for Prosecution would be as my learned friend Mr. Zecevic said. They are free to give us a list of -- formulation of adjudicated facts. In relation to this case, in relation to -- to -- to -- to their case, in relation to -- to -- to proofs and evidence so far and then we shall discuss and see whether we could agree on certain issues. Simply as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, could you -- obviously this is something that the Chamber is going to have to give some further careful thought to. But do I understand your position, and when I say "your," I mean you and Mr. Zecevic, that notwithstanding the ruling that the Trial Chamber may have made on the Prosecution's application -- well, on the application, that certain facts are treated as adjudicated facts, there is, nevertheless, an affirmative burden on the Prosecution, having been given notice of the general objection by the Defence that, in the course of the Prosecution's case, it must, as it were, prove these matters because of that challenge. Is that a fair summary of what I understand your position to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. There is exactly the -- our position, that we -- that we articulated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... seek a ruling on this because, Your Honours, that is not what the decision, the only appeals decision on this, with Judge Shahabuddeen says. It is for the Defence to raise credible and reliable evidence if -- if the above --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I appreciate your position, Ms. Korner. It's just that I wanted to be sure that I was hearing what I thought I was hearing from the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I make it clear. I mean, we did -- we served, and Mr. Pantelic knows this, we spent a considerable amount of time because we were invited to do that by Judge Harhoff and the Defence drafting what we thought were a set of unobjectionable facts to which we hoped the Defence could agree, and we were told in terms that they would not agree them, and they were the most basic ones, and, therefore, we do not propose -- and Mr. Pantelic makes it sound as though the Defence are being reasonable -- we had a refusal, we don't propose to waste any more time, drafting -- spending -- writing out matters which the Defence won't agree. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I may just add a comment on this matter. The thing that hurts is the consequence of this dispute; namely, that we shall have to prolong the trial for a considerable time, in order to deal with matters that really are not subject to any substantial disagreement. And it is for the accused also, both of you, to consider your positions on this issue. Now, if I look at the adjudicated facts, just as an example, the ones that relate to the current witness, and I see adjudicated fact number 1264, it reads as follows: "According to the 1991 census in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ethnic composition in Doboj municipality was 40 per cent Muslims, 39 per cent Serbs, and 13 per cent Croats with the indication of the number of persons, and so-and-so many persons of other -- or unknown ethnicity." Now, the position of the Defence forces the Prosecution to adduce evidence to sustain and support this fact, and it also forces the Chamber to consider the reliability of this fact. So time could be saved if the Defence were able to say, We have no objection against this fact. So that's one-off the number of facts that the Prosecution must then deal with. In other words, there has to be a way in which the parties can get together and sort out and identify the issues that are really subject to disagreement. And once these facts have been identified, then I think, according to the Appeals Chamber's ruling, it would be for the Defence to produce relevant and credible evidence to rebut these facts. But, again, I'm appealing to the parties to -- to continue their efforts to try and weed out all the facts which we don't have to deal with during this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Judge Delvoie reminded me, and I'm perfectly in agreement, that if the Appeals Chamber's decision is to be read consistently, then it would be insufficient for the Defence just to challenge the adjudicated facts of which the Chamber has taken judicial notice on a very general scale. You have to be the one that puts up relevant and credible evidence to rebut the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, the way we read the decision, the appeals decision, is that what is expected of Defence is to challenge the adjudicated facts during the Prosecution case. And in the Defence case, we bring the credible evidence to counter that. That is -- that is the -- in -- in our position, that is the proper reading of -- of -- of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because we would not be -- we would not be able to produce the -- the evidence during the Prosecution case. That's, first of all. The second, the burden of proof is with the Prosecution. And I see Ms. Korner agrees with my assessment and my reading of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do. I mean, that -- that must be right. The problem arises, and it is because of the Lukic decision, we say it is not enough to say we challenge it. There has to be reliable and credible evidence, and there must be some indication that there is reliable and credible evidence. But our position is difficult because if we say -- we're put on notice because there's a specific challenge through a witness to -- or to adjudicate in fact by cross-examination it has to be indicated. It's not enough to say we challenge it. It has to be put to a witness, for example, that -- that -- that the ethnic composition -- let's take a silly example, but the ethnic composition is wrong, and -- of Doboj. And then we're put on notice and that's been put in cross-examination, but the trouble is because of the Lukic decision, if we had been put on notice properly by cross-examinations rather than a blanket, We challenge everything, do we have to, as part of our case, seek to call evidence to deal with it; or can we wait until the Defence case and then call rebuttal evidence? And the Lukic evidence says, no, we can't. So effectively that is why I'm saying it is important that we know what is challenged in advance and for Your Honours to know so that we can look for the witness that covers that particular adjudicated fact if it is important. I mean, obviously if it is important and material to -- to a real issue in the case and then apply to Your Honours regrettably because of this challenge and because there's been a suggestion in cross-examination but without any indication of what -- what the evidence is, to say, we need to call a witness or put in another document. And the only way a trial can proceed efficiently, which is one of the -- of the many aspects of general human rights law, that we should know in advance. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Hence the practicality of the suggestion that Judge Harhoff has made. As the one way of dealing with this, and clearly this was a -- this is not a decided view -- view of the Chamber, is for the parties to get together -- because we're dealing with a large number of facts here, and the difference between the sides on this issue are not as -- as -- as wide as they first appeared. It's merely arriving at a practical means of -- of -- of the -- well, in this case the Prosecution, knowing which of the facts are facts that -- that are -- in such dispute as this evidence has to be called, and, as I said, that is something that we're going to have give further thought to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say, I mean, I don't know how often I have to repeat this, because there's fairness and there's fairness. Judge Harhoff invited us to do just that pre-trial, and we sent -- we have copies of it, we can provide Your Honours, and we may have done so, in fact, I believe, to Judge Harhoff of what we -- we asked the Defence to agree, and we were met with a blanket refusal. Now, having said that, I think Your Honours should make it clear it is for the Defence now to take the initiative and say what they will agree as opposed to what they won't agree, whichever way round it is. We are receptive. We are anxious that we should not have to rehash matters which have been through countless cases and be the subject of countless appeal decisions. I mean, particularly when we get to Prijedor, which is an enormous municipality, as far as the events are concerned, and has been investigated as somebody once put it, there isn't a snail that hasn't been investigated in Prijedor. It has been through seven different cases. We seriously ought to be able, at this stage of the Tribunal's life, to reach agreement on what has been proved beyond a peradventure and concentrate on the real issues; namely, what part did Zupljanin play in those events, what part did Stanisic, what was their knowledge. That is what the issues should be. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We're halfway into this morning's session, the first session for the morning, and obviously this is not a matter that is going to be resolved now, and it's something to which we are going to have to return. Thank you. If there are no further matters, could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Petrovic. Before Mr. Cvijetic continues, I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Petrovic. We broke off yesterday before we called a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please see 65 ter 2387. I apologise if it has been admitted in the meantime. I don't think so, but ... anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is P1345, from our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, this is a report of activities of the Doboj police detachment. This was shown to you by the Prosecution during their examination-in-chief. Do you remember that this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We will reach the last page yet. But I can remind you that this was signed by the detachment commander, Mr. Djukic, I believe was his name, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here's what I would like to discuss with you. During the examination yesterday, I showed you documents and orders of the minister of the interior. And during the examination-in-chief, you were able to see minutes -- or, rather, reports about the inspections of the MUP when the inspectors came to Doboj. What you were able to see from the order, I believe, you will agree with me, is that in his orders, the minister deals with the reduction of the number of members of the reserve police force and giving that excess number to the army to dispose with, and he also deals with the disbanding of all so-called special and other units that were established during the war without his orders. They, too, are placed at the disposal of the army. The minister, in his order, informs the recipients that the establishment of a special police detachment at Pale is in progress and that it was being manned. I suppose that you know that only the minister has the power to establish such units under the law. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you said yourself that this detachment was established by Major Stankovic, if I'm not mistake, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that it was really he who enlarged the number of reserve police officer so that a great many of them -- so that such a detachment, such a very strong detachment could be established, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed that the funding normally came from the municipal -- municipal funds or the municipal budget and that the Crisis Staff decided that this should be done that way.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to the following page in this document. One -- one more, page 3, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, let me turn your attention to the first two sentences. This says that the detachment was established on 8 May 1992, right? But later on, there's a sentence that the Defence thinks is wrong - I'm saying this for the record - it says that, pursuant to a decision, an order of the ministry the number of members was reduced from 1300 to 720, and so on. Bearing in mind what we said in this introductory part and yesterday, obviously the minister had nothing to do with the detachment, with that unit because he didn't even know of its existence when it was being established. Rather, the minister dealt with what he was authorised to do under the law. Namely, the reserve police force, its strength, and the ratio between the regular police force and the reserve police force. You remember that this -- this was what one of his documents said, correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he knew it or didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting the position of the Defence to you that he was dealing with the reserve police rather than the detachment. Did you find information anywhere to show that he dealt with this detachment? I don't think so. Neither have I. The crux of the matter, Mr. Petrovic, is that the minister's order to disband this kind of a unit and similar units was not implemented on time and the reserve police force was not reduced in strength in a timely fashion. You will agree with me that this was one of the -- this is one -- one of the things that were put to you yesterday and you put forward the reasons why it wasn't done in time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that everybody knew of the existence of this detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would suggest that we go to page 5 of the document. I'm referring to the page in the B/C/S version. I apologise, I can't give the page reference in English, but I believe it's the same. The last paragraph in the B/C/S says that the detachment wasn't being helped by the ministry in any way - that's the very last paragraph - or, rather, the last-but-one paragraph and the second sentence in that paragraph. Not receiving any help at all from the Republika Srpska MUP for the covering of the stations' expenses and also the maintenance of the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could we now please go to the last page of the document before I put my next question to you. That's the section where the proposed conclusions are listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may have to turn back one page because that's where it starts; although the very last ones are more interesting to me. This is the page. In English, it is probably also one page back. We'll just find the conclusions in English, probably on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It starts in the lower part of the page. The author of this text lists conclusions as a summary of what precedes, and in the last part, we can see the proposed measures for the improvement of the security situation. Mr. Petrovic, please read what the author of this document proposes.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean under 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, just read everything.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please go to the end of the document. Yes, 7, 8, 9, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you at least agree with me when I say that all these proposed measures are targeted at local bodies, municipal bodies, from whom certain actions are requested, help, et cetera. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's what it says. You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that the document doesn't show to who it was sent. But I suppose you will agree with me that a logical conclusion would that be it was drafted for the local authorities from whom help is requested.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, my question actually is whether or not the only logical conclusion is that what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Probably, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is already in evidence, there's no need to tender it. I can pass onto the following document. Could we please see 65 ter 2775. Could we please turn to the next page immediately. This is just a file sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, this is a letter from the chief of the centre, Andrija Bjelosevic, who sent this letter to all stations, including yours, forwarding the minister's order that we have already commented on. I mean the one about the implementation of detention measures, by which I mean the three days, which is the duration of remand prison that you were authorised to impose. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to the next page. Attached there's the minister's order. This is the original that we read yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember? Can you remember whether you received Mr. Bjelosevic's -- this order of Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can't remember, very well. Well, if you can't remember, I cannot tender this document, and the minister's order is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's move on to the next document, 65 ter 190. I think it was also admitted as P590.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a document that the Prosecution has also showed you. It's about the problems with regard to the activities of paramilitary units in the territory of the Doboj CSB. You read it with the OTP. I believe that are you familiar with the contents. So let us comment on the third paragraph now. It starts with: "These groups benefit from ..." et cetera. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember with -- what the chief of the centre is saying about the problems he's pointing out and because of which it is difficult to put these paramilitaries under control? Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And he goes on to propose measures to be taken. You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to the next page, please. Let's just wait for it to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please focus your attention on the lower part of the page. It's about the problem the police is facing in -- in combat. Do read it and then we'll comment on it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree what Mr. Bjelosevic says here?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the problem he's pointing out here, about the use of these men and the problems connected with it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is saying that they are using the police when necessary; and when not, the police, again, stays under military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have this paragraph which has been marked. If can you read it, it says: "A commission was formed recently at the Crisis Staff level ..." Please read it. You can confirm the accuracy of this information, because you spoke about the commission for triage and for the release of persons from detention. My question is: Did the CSB get actively involved in the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There was?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this has been admitted, too, I will not need it any longer. Thank you. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D00-2306.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: See this? This is from the Security Services Centre. It was sent to your station, and they request certain information to be compiled. Would you please look at this and then give us your comments. Have you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can turn to the last page to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Andrija Bjelosevic, chief of the centre, signed it, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this letter, and was something done pursuant to the letter of the chief of the centre?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But, most likely we did receive it, and we were supposed to produce a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you can't help me in answering pursuant to his -- to whose request this information was compiled. What is relevant for you is simply that you had to act upon this letter of the centre, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So can you confirm that you, nevertheless, received this document and that you acted in accordance with it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now turn to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before you turn to another subject, I think it would be interesting to see the results of the inquiry that Mr. Bjelosevic made. The witness said that he thinks that they actually did receive it and that they replied. But what was the answers given to the inquiry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, do you know what were the results of the inquiry; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence will have to make its own inquiry. We will have to contact and get information from the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... obviously. Because one thing is that the CSB is asking for this information. But if we don't know the answer, then I'm not sure what use the Chamber is to make of this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expected the witness to know and to remember, but now that he says that he doesn't know and he doesn't remember, it is clear that we will have to make further inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, in the course of examination-in-chief, questions were put to you about - if I may say so - the investigation of crimes which took place in the territory under the jurisdiction of your centre. You will agree with me that the atmosphere which persisted in Doboj was suitable for commission of various crime, including the gravest ones?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There was an enormous jump in the number of crimes committed, especially the most serious ones?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the aggravating factor in identifying and locating the perpetrators was the fact that in the territory of Doboj municipality, there emerged some unidentified persons concerning whom you had no intelligence. These people stayed there briefly and then left the territory of the municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you giving evidence, Mr. Cvijetic, the way that question was phrased?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In investigating the crimes was this fact that we just mentioned a hindrance in that process?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was it a hindrance, also, that they frequently disguised themselves in different uniforms and that it wasn't really clear to whom they belonged, to what group, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, you said that in relation to all documented crimes, on-site investigations were carried out, evidence was secured, and investigations were conducted. Did I interpret your answers correctly?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, that wasn't the case. But later on when the services were established, they started working on investigating the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the information we read a bit earlier on, in relation to this initial period, it was said that you had technical problems, personnel problems, and various other problems in doing your work, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, crimes which were committed at that time by unidentified perpetrators had to be documented as well. And then, later on, they were supposed to investigate, in order to identify the perpetrators, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In cases where perpetrators were identified, the records were completed and sent to the prosecutor's office, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is this how they proceeded, once you got organised, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once we got organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this work in your police station was performed by your crime protection services for minor crimes; and in the centre, they had their own service, which dealt with the most serious crimes. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I showed you a set of criminal reports, some against known and some against unknown perpetrators, all signed by Mr. Bjelosevic. But you told us that since this was done by crime investigation services, that this was their line of work, you couldn't really be of assistance to me in relation to specific cases. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For the sake of showing an example, I will put to you two documents, and perhaps you could assist us, if you remember anything about these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have three minutes left and two documents. I can't possibly complete them in three minutes. Perhaps it would be a good idea to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As a matter of courtesy to counsel and the accused, I would explain that our delay in resuming the Bench was due to certain housekeeping matters that we're trying to sort out. The fruits of our discussions counsel would learn in the course of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we now call on the screen 1D01-0349, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before the break, and also earlier, we spoke about identifying and pressing charges for crimes committed in the territory of Doboj municipality. Here, I have a document that, so to speak, lists the crimes committed by unidentified perpetrators. As I was able to see, there is also a record of crimes where the victims were non-Serbs. Do you see this too?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, what is this document? Is it a SJB report or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suppose this is a report of a CSB, not a SJB. And this is what I wanted to clarify with the witness, whether he can identify this document and confirm its authenticity. And I won't tender it until we ensure all this information. So my goal was exactly what you just asked about. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, what you can see in this document is that there is an record, a compilation, of all crimes committed by -- by unidentified persons against non-Serbs. Do you see this as well?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, if I may return to the query raised by Judge Harhoff, should you prove the document first before you put the contents to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to elicit the information on the document from the witness. I will ask him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could this be a report of a CSB given the gravity of the crimes it mentions? Because your SJB did not deal with this type of crime. Can you assist me there?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this document could be coming from a CSB, not from your SJB, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the cases mentioned here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all -- we don't have any date on this document. We don't have -- we don't who the maker is. And the date is very relevant when this was made so I don't know if we can have any information. Where was this obtained, how, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There is apparently no signature on this document. So before asking any further questions, can we maybe establish the foundations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The only thing the witness says, Mr. Cvijetic, is that this is not a SJB document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he allowed -- or, rather, he conceded that this might be a document of the CSB if I'm not mistake. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it might be anything, if I may say so with respect. The issue, as I said, Judge Harhoff first alerted you to and Mr. Demirdjian has now raised that, before we -- I expect at the end of the exercise you would seek to be eliciting evidence from the witness which the Chamber should take on board in terms of evaluating the contents of this document, but before we get to that, there is a fundamental question of what the document is, and it isn't helpful to ask questions [indiscernible] what it could be, because it could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. I will not deal with the document, but instead I will ask the witnesses about the cases mentioned in it. I wasn't going to tender the document anyway because I still cannot provide what you ask of me. I will no longer deal with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is we're going back to the same thing. Unless Mr. Cvijetic can tell the Court where this document comes from, what it is supposed to be, he cannot ask questions based upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I've already said I wouldn't be discussing the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that the document be removed from the screen and I will ask questions without referring to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, so this document is not related to the document. Were an on-site investigations made and was evidence collected about crimes, the victims of which were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did your crime investigation service distinguish with regard to the ethnicity of the victim when it comes to what they should do?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the earlier days, it wasn't done, but, later on, we did do it, regardless of the ethnicity of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would like to call up the following document which we will be able to identify. It's 1D03 -- 1D03-1240.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you said twice that you did not do it; but later on, when the conditions were favourable and possibly when you were able to do it, or trained to do it, then you would engage in that activity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this is a criminal report for a specific crime, the victim of which was Ivan Cigoj. Judging by the name, we can conclude that he is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And Ferid Cabric probably Muslim?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the perpetrator is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the criminal report went to the public prosecutor's office of the Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this case?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just look at the last page of this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here you can see a list of attachments to the criminal report. To the extent you know - and you said that your crime investigation service dealt with this - is this the usual way of completing a criminal report, once the -- the required activities have been done?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you said you don't know about this specific case, I will not tender this document. Instead, I will move on to the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 65 ter 964.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we're now passing onto another topic. You have been asked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Which tab is this on your list? I'm just trying to find the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40 in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were asked about communications and communicating with the headquarters; that is, the MUP. I asked you about that. And I found a statement of yours that it was your impression that the MUP was actually in existence and functioned as of August 1992. Do you remember that this was your estimate?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that that was the month when you started receiving orders from the MUP, and in August an inspection from the MUP arrived to your area, and that made you conclude that after -- after the corridor was cut through -- or, rather, after the corridor was established, things started functioning and communications were possible.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only possible after the corridor was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After that, a document was shown to you that the stations were submitting daily reports to the ministry. Do you remember the Prosecutor showing you that in the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then take a look at one of these daily reports. I believe we have it on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let us turn to the last page. In the English version, it seems we'll have to scroll up to the last paragraph on the last-but-one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read this remark, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No. It doesn't have to be aloud.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that this corroborates what you said; that this -- that for this daily report from Doboj, information was not received in the period you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you don't know this document, that you haven't seen it, apart from confirming what I've asked you? Therefore, I'll show you the next daily report, for which the Defence established that was the first daily report, including information from the Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see Exhibit 65 ter 995. It is also marked as P170.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a bulletin. We see that it's dated 24 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to the last page in both linguistic versions. And could we enlarge the last paragraph which refers to Doboj. It may be difficult to read it, but I think it's legible after all. It says Serbian municipality of Doboj, and some sort of explosion is mentioned and an on-site investigation. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is barely legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, it says, various goods are taken away on a large scale, and persons in uniform are mentioned. And do read the last sentence. "Equipment belonging to the Derventa SJB has been taken away," and so on. So, can you see what I've just read to you, the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The first information to draft such a bulletin -- at least that is my conclusion based on my perusal of all the bulletins, and I've read them all, was received after the corridor was established after the 24th of June [as interpreted]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 24 July, if this could be corrected, please. And the document also reads 24th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Speaking about means of communication, let us see a 65 ter document, 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I wasn't sure what the purpose was of showing this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness was shown a document, and he was required to say whether or not they were duty-bound to send information to the MUP from the municipality of Doboj about the events in that municipality. This has to do with the issue of the existence or non-existence of communication lines with the ministry. I just tried to confirm what the witness has said, that only after the establishment of the corridor, this manner of informing the MUP became possible only as of 24 July 1992, which date can be seen here. The following document also has to do with this, but it isn't a bulletin. So, Your Honour, I'm actually talking about the setting up of communication lines with the Ministry of the Interior. May I continue, Your Honours, with the following document? Can we see that 65 ter 68 document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I, again, would ask you to read it before I ask you about it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the author? So this the Department of Communications and Cryptographic Protection. Do you know the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the signature down there should be his, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The information from this report, from the 30th of July until the 30th of September, does it look familiar to you? Do you know about the problems in the communications that this document speaks of? You've mentioned it yourself.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were problem, but I don't know about this specific information. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In this document, it says that it wasn't until this period - from the 30th of July until the 30th of September - that they started solving the problems with the communications and that they started establishing at least some basic communication channels but that, however, some problems remained and that they were working on them. Do you see what it says here?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You must know that the basic type of communication in the police work is a dispatch or a teleprinter type of communication.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Based on this document, I can't see that teleprinter connection was established and they mostly relied on telephone and fax communication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, we have previously reminded you that you're counsel, not witness in this matter, so please ask questions of the witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, do you see in this document on what type of communication the people who worked at the CSB relied on?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I see it in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Telephone and telegraph. It's added in handwriting, telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You weren't clear. Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, it says that they used telephone. It says that they established telephone connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And, based on your recollection, was that the only type of communication in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Based on your answer, it is clear that the dispatch type of communication is missing, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, other than confirming the author and the authenticity of this document, can you also confirm that the content of this document is accurate?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right then. We will have to cover this with somebody else. Mr. Petrovic, I would like us to go back to two documents that have already been put to you. 65 ter 1274, which has become P1341, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 3 in the B/C/S. That's the last page, so it should be easy to find it in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the paragraph which begins with the words: "Before the arrival of inspector Cedo Tosic ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the inspectors from the Ministry of Interior, by way of this document, request the exact numbers of both regular police force and reserve force?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in this paragraph, we can see why they need this: In order to plan accurately the funds for payments. Is that your interpretation too?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you a document of yours, in which you inform, I think in October, that you established police stations of reserve force. But in that document, you say that it wasn't easy to reduce the number of reserve policemen down to the number requested by the ministry, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was that number harmonised with the number requested by the minister while you were chief of police?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll show you another document put to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 304. It is P405 now, if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I was just asking about the significance of the evidence that you just elicited with the last documents and the witness. What is the significance of the order to reduce the number of police officers in the Doboj SJB? What's the impacts that you wish to show?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, based on the regulations of Republika Srpska, and also internal regulations of the Ministry of the Interior, there is an established ratio between the number of active and reserve policemen. In the territory of Doboj municipality, for the reasons that this witness discussed, there was an enormous increase in the number of reserve policemen. The Ministry of the Interior, following the arrival of its inspectors in Doboj, requested that they abide by the ratio and that they harmonise the number with the one required by the ministry. This is one of the problems, on account of which the inspectors intervened, and this was a criticism sent by the ministry both to the CSB and to the SJB. Namely, that they didn't comply with the regulations of the ministry by the deadline given to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And -- and what do you -- what's the point of drawing this conclusion? What does this show in relation to the case against your client? Why is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the reasons for removing Mr. Petrovic from office was precisely that. When giving evidence about this, he said that he accepted his share of responsibility, but he also said that he wasn't the only one responsible for that kind of a situation in Doboj. You must remember this evidence of his. My other goal in doing this was that I wanted to show that the ministry, as soon as it was physically able to reach Doboj, tried to regulate the situation, both at the SJB and CSB, so that it would be in compliance with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, this is not contested by the Prosecution, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. And we don't see the link with the crimes that are charged in the indictment either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have stated my position. I simply wanted to show that the ministry, whenever it was in the position to reach any part of the territory of Republika Srpska, attempted to ensure that the regulations of Republika Srpska and internal regulations of the ministry concerning its organisational units, were complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Cvijetic, but I think it would be useful to point out to you that there is a request to both parties in this and other trials before this Tribunal, to focus, really, on the evidence that is necessary and relevant to the cases that are tried before us. And -- and this would be one instances where I would say, you know, you shouldn't have taken up time to -- to deal with this issue. I mean, it's really not necessary, it's not relevant, as far as can I see. So here's one example of time that you could have saved and focussed on something more relevant and directly useful to the trial. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before Mr. Cvijetic continues could I ask the Court how much time Mr. Cvijetic plans on using, because we have another witness waiting, and I plan on having re-examination of somewhere between a half-hour and 45 minutes. So it would be good to know for the purposes of the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm about to ask my very last questions to this witness, and I will no longer discuss this document. Then I'll finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, at the beginning of the war you said Doboj was divided, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That division was made along ethnic lines, as it were, considering the -- the -- the ethnic affiliation of the majority of the population of a certain area, right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did that division from that period persist, and was it also confirmed by the Dayton Peace Accord?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the town, which was inhabited by 30 per cent of Serbs and 70 per cent of non-Serbs, the -- that is, Doboj south, Doboj east, and the Usora municipality, were also so regulated by Dayton.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the interpreters didn't catch your last sentence, so would you be good enough to repeat it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Doboj east is concerned and Doboj south and Usora, the municipality of Usora, they are in the outskirts of town, and they remained in that framework. Whereas, the town itself out of 35.000 inhabitant, 70 per cent were non-Serbs and 30 per cent were Serbs. Those 70 per cent left Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How many Dobojs are there now?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doboj east, Doboj south, and the Usora municipality, half of which belonged to Doboj, and the other half to Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That means that one municipality was split in four. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now my question is whether, in the territory of Doboj, which remained part of Republika Srpska, to put it that way, was it populated -- or has it been populated by Serb refugees from other areas, especially Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When did that happen? Right at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From before the war until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you have information about the number of persons involved?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly about 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it still the position of counsel for Zupljanin that they have no cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, as I announced, I have about half an hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may begin [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrovic. Yesterday you were shown the rules on the disciplinary responsibility in the MUP. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday? Yes, I remember. It was shown to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this was Exhibit 1D54.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could display it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if you remember, the Defence read to you a number of articles from those disciplinary rules. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From what I remember, you were shown a number of articles. 1, 2, 3, and 4, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to page 7 in the English version and page 4 in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, these questions were put to you in relation to your dismissal, and one article that was not shown to you was Article 8. If you could take a few seconds to read that article. And for the record, this article says that: "In order for a request to initiate a procedure to establish disciplinary responsibility for serious violations of work duty to be filed, the worker must be questioned and other evidence obtained?" Do you see that, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to 1992, were you ever questioned?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you look at the next article, which is Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And we will need to go to the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You can see Article 9 on the screen, Mr. Petrovic. And it says: "A request to initiate disciplinary procedures shall be delivered to the accused." Was anything of that sort delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And from the beginning of 1992 until you heard of this meeting in October 1992, did you receive any warning, whether written or verbal, about your performance as a SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm done with that document. We can put it away. Let me ask you, Mr. Petrovic: In the Ministry of Interior, who is responsible for the appointment of CSB chiefs and SJB chiefs?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the centre makes a proposal to the minister also for removal. And the minister makes a decision about either removal or appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at page 9916 the Defence put to you that you were not removed by the minister. And we saw the document of the 18th of January, 1993, which came from the minister. Now, did that document effectively remove you from your position?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my position, that a meeting was held with -- at General Lisica's office in September, and I saw the document in October 1992. Last year, in September, I saw a document, a proposal, by the chief of the centre to -- to the minister that I be removed as -- stating that I didn't introduce order but not mentioning that I did not downsize the police. And the third item, I believe, was that I protected staff of Muslim ethnicity. Muslims. And I heard that those people were subsequently dismissed from the SJB. As soon as I get that document, I'll give it to the Prosecutor, because it was only shown to me last year in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to this, could we show Exhibit P625 which is the annual report of the RS MUP for the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, you haven't seen -- you probably have not seen this document before. But I would like you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like us to go to page 38 in the B/C/S version, which is page 27 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the section 4, which is: Organisation, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you look at the third paragraph, which starts with the sentence: "In implementing personnel policies, the starting points were primarily Serbian patriotism and professionalism ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you comment on this, in the light of what you told us about the way you were removed from your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness knows nothing about the document and still is required to comment and speculate on who had what on their minds when writing this sentence. And, anyway, this is something I never dealt with in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, in the same way that I queried Mr. Cvijetic's dealing with a number of documents which speak for themselves and questioning the utility of asking a witness don't you agree that the document says, what -- well, there are two objections that Mr. Cvijetic has raised. One is this doesn't come out of cross-examination and that the -- whether the witness is capable of even commenting on this. How does that assist -- how does the first objection -- the first question is: How does it assist us, and in any event, does this arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In relation to the first part of the objection, yes, it does. I believe Mr. Cvijetic challenged the witness on the reasons of his removal. As for part two, this is the annual report of the RS MUP, an organisation to which the witness belonged in 1992, and it describes the policy of how personnel matters were resolved in 1992, and here is a witness who can talk about the way he was removed. I will not dwell on this document too long, Your Honours. I just want him to comment as to the policy within the RS MUP, to which he was a subject of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may ask that question directly. Because you need his reaction to this -- notwithstanding the statement that appears, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, let me repeat my question then. What is your comment, in light of what you told us, about the way you were removed?

utterances.speaker: OBREN PETROVIC [Resumed]
